edits.english: A burnt offering is a gift: It does not come to atone for a positive commandment directly, but rather, after repentance has atoned for the positive commandment, it comes for receiving favor, like a person who sinned against a king and appeased him through advocates, and when he comes to greet him, he brings a gift with him.
What are the circumstances: That is, what are the circumstances for it to come as an atonement?
If there is no repentance: For transgressions of positive commandments that he committed.
The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination: This is a verse in Proverbs (21).

These matters raise a question that early and later commentators discussed in various ways: According to this, what is the meaning of the statements made above that a burnt offering atones for positive mitzvot? Ba'al ha-Turim in his commentary on the Torah (Leviticus 1:4) wrote that even though, as stated here, when one repents, he is forgiven, nevertheless, the atonement is not complete until he brings a burnt offering. The Ramban, however, wrote in his commentary on the Torah (Leviticus 1:4) that those liable for intentional violations of positive mitzvot, even though no punishment is decreed upon them in the Torah, nevertheless, they transgressed God's will and are not favored before Him, and the burnt offering brought as a gift — through it, he becomes favored before God and atoned. From Rashi's words here, it appears that even though it is said that a burnt offering atones for positive mitzvot — the intention is not for actual atonement (i.e., the actual forgiveness of the sin, cleansing the person from the sin), because this has already been fully accomplished through repentance, but rather it involves atonement in the sense that through it, the sinner appeases God when he wishes to see His face (and this is also one of the meanings of the term atonement, like "I will appease his face with a gift... and after that, I will see his face" (Genesis 32:21). See also in Iggeret HaTeshuva by the Baal HaTanya, Chapter 2).

From the Greek <greek>δῶρον</greek> (doron), meaning gift or present. Some wrote that perhaps the primary atonement of the burnt offering is for positive commandments that one neglected unwittingly, and for which he did not repent (for this, the disqualification of "sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination" is not applicable) (Ḥazon Yeḥezkel).
One who violated a positive mitzva (that is not punishable by karet) and repented — is forgiven immediately. (Rambam Sefer HaMadda, Hilkhot Teshuva 1:4).
The origin of the word is in Greek <greek>δῶρον</greek> (doron) — a gift, an offering.
A burnt offering is a gift: Even though a positive commandment atones more than a sin offering, since it atones by implication.
